lessons.title: Real numbers: rational or irrational
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to classify real numbers as rational or irrational.
lessons.explanation: Rational numbers can be written as a fraction of two integers, with a non-zero denominator. Integers, terminating decimals and recurring decimals are rational. A square root is rational only when its radicand is a perfect square. Numbers such as √2 and π are real but irrational.
lessons.workedExample:
Classify √81.
1. 81 is a perfect square: 9 × 9 = 81.
2. √81 = 9.
3. 9 is an integer, so it is rational.
Therefore √81 is a rational real number.
lessons.misconception: A root sign does not automatically mean “irrational”. Check whether the number inside the root is a perfect square.

practiceQuestions.solution: 20 is not a perfect square, so √20 cannot be written as a ratio of integers. The other choices are rational.
practiceQuestions.hint: Check whether the radicand is a perfect square.

lessons.title: Factors, multiples, HCF and LCM
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to use prime factors to find an HCF or LCM.
lessons.explanation: A factor divides a number exactly; a multiple is made by multiplying. Prime factorisation writes a number as primes. For HCF use only common prime factors at their smallest powers. For LCM use every required prime factor at its largest power.
lessons.workedExample:
Find the HCF and LCM of 24 and 36.
24 = 2³ × 3 and 36 = 2² × 3².
HCF = 2² × 3 = 12.
LCM = 2³ × 3² = 72.
lessons.misconception: Do not choose the HCF when a situation asks when repeated events next happen together: that needs the LCM.

lessons.title: Ratio and unit rate
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to simplify a ratio and calculate a unit rate.
lessons.explanation: A ratio compares quantities in the same order. Divide every part by the same common factor to simplify it. A rate compares unlike units, for example kilometres per hour. Find a unit rate by dividing to make one of the quantities equal to one.
lessons.workedExample:
A recipe uses 6 cups flour for 4 cups water.
Divide both parts by 2.
6 : 4 = 3 : 2.
For every 3 cups flour, use 2 cups water.
lessons.misconception: Do not add the numbers in a ratio. A ratio is multiplicative: both parts must scale by the same factor.

distractorExplanations.A: Revisit the worked method: Find a number that divides both parts.
distractorExplanations.B: Revisit the worked method: Find a number that divides both parts.
distractorExplanations.D: Revisit the worked method: Find a number that divides both parts.

practiceQuestions.solution: The HCF of 18 and 24 is 6. Divide both parts: 18 ÷ 6 : 24 ÷ 6 = 3 : 4.
practiceQuestions.hint: Find a number that divides both parts.

lessons.title: Direct and inverse proportion
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to decide whether a situation uses direct or inverse proportion.
lessons.explanation: In direct proportion, both quantities change in the same direction at a constant rate: more items cost more. In inverse proportion, one quantity increases while the other decreases so that their product stays fixed: more equally efficient workers take fewer days.
lessons.workedExample:
Four workers take 15 days.
Total work = 4 × 15 = 60 worker-days.
With 6 workers: 60 ÷ 6 = 10 days.
This is inverse proportion.
lessons.misconception: “One goes up and one goes down” is not enough by itself. The total task or product must stay fixed for inverse proportion.

distractorExplanations.D: Revisit the worked method: Find the cost of one notebook.

practiceQuestions.solution: One notebook costs R40 ÷ 5 = R8. Eight cost 8 × R8 = R64.
practiceQuestions.hint: Find the cost of one notebook.

lessons.title: Commission, rental and compound interest
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to calculate common Grade 9 financial applications.
lessons.explanation: Commission is a percentage of sales. Rental questions often have a per-day amount plus a once-off fee. Compound interest grows the balance each period, so each new percentage is calculated on the previous balance.
lessons.workedExample:
R2 000 earns 10% compound interest for two years.
Year 1: R2 000 × 1.10 = R2 200.
Year 2: R2 200 × 1.10 = R2 420.
The balance is R2 420.
lessons.misconception: Do not add the once-off rental fee once for every day, and do not use simple interest when the question says compound.

lessons.title: Integer operations and order
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to calculate with signed integers using the correct order of operations.
lessons.explanation: For addition and subtraction, use a number line or rewrite subtraction as adding the opposite. For multiplication and division, same signs give a positive answer and different signs give a negative answer. Evaluate brackets before powers, multiplication or division, then addition or subtraction.
lessons.workedExample:

Subtracting a negative is adding its opposite.
−6 − (−9) = −6 + 9 = 3.

lessons.title: Squares, cubes and roots
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to evaluate integer powers and roots.
lessons.explanation: A square multiplies a number by itself; a cube uses three factors. Brackets decide whether a negative sign belongs to the base. √ gives the principal non-negative square root, while cube roots can be negative.
lessons.workedExample:
Evaluate (−4)².
The brackets make −4 the base.
(−4)² = (−4) × (−4) = 16.
lessons.misconception: Without brackets, −4² means −(4²) = −16. The brackets matter.

lessons.title: Exponent laws
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to use product, quotient and power laws for exponents.
lessons.explanation: For the same non-zero base: multiply means add exponents, divide means subtract exponents, and a power of a power means multiply exponents. The base does not change just because the exponent changes.
lessons.workedExample:
Simplify (x³)⁴.
A power of a power multiplies exponents.
(x³)⁴ = x^(3 × 4) = x¹².
lessons.misconception: Do not use the product law for addition: x² + x³ cannot be simplified by adding exponents.

lessons.title: Zero and negative exponents
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to interpret zero and negative exponents.
lessons.explanation: For any non-zero base a, a⁰ = 1. A negative exponent makes a reciprocal: a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ. These follow from the quotient law, for example a³ ÷ a³ = a⁰ = 1.
lessons.misconception: A negative exponent does not make the answer negative. It tells you to use a reciprocal.

lessons.title: Scientific notation extension
lessons.objective: By the end of this optional extension, you should be able to write large and small numbers in scientific notation.
lessons.explanation: Scientific notation writes a number as a × 10ⁿ where 1 ≤ a < 10. Moving the decimal left gives a positive exponent; moving it right gives a negative exponent. This extension supports number sense but is not a required Term 1 mastery prerequisite.

lessons.title: Linear nth-term rules
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to find and test a linear nth-term rule.
lessons.explanation: For a linear pattern, start with Tn = dn + c, where d is the first difference. Substitute n = 1 and the first term to find c. Then test the rule with another term; a rule is only useful if it matches the pattern.
lessons.workedExample:

Difference d = 4, so Tn = 4n + c.
At n = 1: 4 + c = 6, so c = 2.
Rule: Tn = 4n + 2. Check T2 = 10.

lessons.title: Geometric matchstick and tile patterns
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to connect a growing diagram to a table and rule.
lessons.explanation: For a visual pattern, count the first few figures carefully and identify what each new figure adds. In a row of joined squares, the first square uses 4 matchsticks and each extra square shares a side, so it adds 3. The rule is M = 3n + 1.

lessons.title: Grade 8 bridge: factors and order
lessons.objective: By the end of this bridge, you should be able to use factors and the order of operations before returning to Grade 9.
lessons.explanation: Factors divide exactly. In calculations, do brackets first, then multiplication or division, then addition or subtraction. This bridge helps with HCF, LCM and integer work.
lessons.misconception: Working left to right through every symbol ignores the order of operations.

lessons.title: Grade 8 bridge: fractions
lessons.objective: By the end of this bridge, you should be able to add and compare simple fractions.
lessons.explanation: Fractions must have a common denominator before adding or subtracting. Equivalent fractions name the same amount and are made by multiplying numerator and denominator by the same number.

lessons.title: Grade 8 bridge: decimal operations
lessons.objective: By the end of this bridge, you should be able to calculate accurately with decimals.
lessons.explanation: Line up decimal points when adding or subtracting. For multiplication, estimate first and place the decimal after multiplying whole-number digits. Decimals support rates, money and proportional reasoning.

lessons.title: Grade 8 bridge: signed numbers
lessons.objective: By the end of this bridge, you should be able to add, subtract and multiply signed integers.
lessons.explanation: Use a number line for addition and subtraction. For multiplication, matching signs give a positive result; different signs give a negative result. These ideas support Grade 9 integer calculations.
lessons.workedExample:
Calculate −3 + 8.
Start at −3.
Move 8 steps right.
The answer is 5.

lessons.title: Grade 8 bridge: exponent basics
lessons.objective: By the end of this bridge, you should be able to read powers and use the product law with the same base.
lessons.explanation: An exponent tells how many equal factors are multiplied. For the same base, multiplication adds exponents. This is the foundation for Grade 9 zero and negative exponents.
lessons.workedExample:

The base is 3 in both terms.
Add exponents: 2+4=6.
Answer: 3⁶.
lessons.misconception: Exponents are not ordinary numbers to multiply when bases are being multiplied.

lessons.title: Grade 8 bridge: simple pattern rules
lessons.objective: By the end of this bridge, you should be able to extend a simple number pattern and test a rule.
lessons.explanation: Find how a pattern changes, then use a table to test a proposed rule. A constant first difference means that each new term adds the same number.
